Code for reproducibility is available at https://github.com/SiamakGhodsi/FairPGT.

papers.title: What Interpolators Store and What They Express: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Benign Overfitting and Label-Free Model Selection
papers.authors: Nikolaos Nikolaou
papers.summary: Overparameterized learners can fit noisy training labels perfectly and still predict well, which neither classical complexity measures nor information-theoretic generalization bounds explain. We develop an information-theoretic framework that separates two things an interpolating learner does with its sample: storage, the information the trained model retains about its training labels, and expression, the information about the sample that reaches its predictions at fresh inputs. We first characterize the ideal model: for a loss l, the least complex l-sufficient representation is the Bayes act, whose entropy is the minimal sufficient complexity; this generalizes, and corrects, an earlier "lossless maximal compression" view of boosting. We then show that every interpolator stores exactly nH(Y|X) bits of label noise, so storage, and bounds built on it (including CMI bounds), cannot tell interpolators apart. Expression can: excess risk is bounded above and below by the expressed information V, the entropy over training samples of the prediction at an input, plus a modal-bias term, exactly so for binary labels. Benign overfitting is therefore vanishing expression, a picture that covers nearest-neighbour rules, averaging, minimum-norm least squares and double descent, and that links V to classical bias-variance decompositions and to model disagreement. Finally, V gives a model-selection criterion that needs no held-out labels. Among overparameterized learners on 15 noisy datasets, V estimated from two disjoint halves has 60% less regret than holdout validation at the same cost and matches 5-fold cross-validation at a quarter of its cost; at matched cost it also beats selection by conditional mutual information. We characterize when it fails and give remedies. Code: https://github.com/nnikolaou/GLMC

papers.title: LoRN: Low-Rank Noise Steering for Generative Robot Policies
papers.authors: Wei Liu, Abrar Anwar, Huihua Zhao, Soha Pouya et al.
papers.summary: Noise steering improves pretrained generative robot policies by learning to select their initial noise without updating model weights. We find that actions in the evaluated world-action models are more sensitive to video noise than action noise, making video noise an expressive input for steering. However, the noise-steering methods we evaluate, in their published forms, struggle to scale to the high-dimensional noise inputs of large policy classes such as world-action models. We introduce Low-Rank Noise Steering (LoRN), a reinforcement learning method that scales noise steering to world-action models. A small steering actor selects a direction through a fixed low-rank random projection, while our norm-controlled construction keeps the resulting noise near the typical scale of a Gaussian sample. This separates the actor's control dimension from the full noise dimension, enabling steering of both video and action inputs. Across three world-action models and ten model-task pairs, video steering improves average success by 26.2 percentage points over the base policy, compared with 7.1 points for DSRL action steering. For smaller action policies, the same construction achieves comparable final success while generally improving early-training success. Steering actors trained in simulation also transfer to three physical bimanual manipulation tasks across two base policies, without additional real-world training.

papers.title: Agent Verifiers in Counterfactual Analysis: A Pilot Study Benchmarking Agentic Heterogeneous Treatment Effects
papers.authors: Satiyabooshan Murugaboopathy, Entejar Alam, Adel Daoud, Connor T. Jerzak
papers.summary: Agents can expand the covariate space of randomized experiments by retrieving fast-moving local context missed by slow-changing survey baseline covariates, helping characterize who benefits most from an intervention. Verifying such covariates is difficult: individual treatment effects are unobserved, retrieval leakage can pull post-treatment information into nominally pretreatment summaries, and encoder leakage can inject post-treatment pretraining knowledge into representations even after temporal filtering of inputs. Guided by a two-channel information bound separating summary provenance from encoder weights, we propose a three-layer benchmark protocol: (i) retrieval admissibility via pre-treatment date filtering; (ii) heterogeneity validation scored rank-weighted average treatment effects (RATEs); and (iii) encoder admissibility checked with chronologically vintaged encoders, future-fact probes, and weight perturbations. Across 11 datasets anchored by Uganda's Youth Opportunities Program, we compare session-isolated retrieval (sandboxed, bounded-budget agent runs per study) against a persistent workspace teammate (xAI's GrokBot) that builds one date-verified corpus per study while blinded to outcomes. The workspace teammate yields higher mean RATE ratios in 6/11 datasets for text alone and 7 for combined features, though paired tests show neither workflow universally dominates. Even on fixed retrieved text, encoder choice significantly shifts heterogeneity signal. Chronologically vintaged probes show no clear evidence of weight leakage, but single-record adapter perturbation analyses show that memorized future facts, once present, persist until injected noise degrades model output. Temporal filtering of retrieval is necessary but insufficient: verifying agent-generated covariates requires jointly examining source provenance, out-of-sample treatment-effect signal, and encoder weights.

papers.title: How Uncertain Is My Action? Self-Correcting Visual Planning with Frozen World Models
papers.authors: Siqing Li, Luming Yang, Yijia Jiao, Junze Deng et al.
papers.summary: A frozen latent world model combined with sampling-based model predictive control is a visual planner. At deployment, the executed action can depart from the commanded one, and the frozen model has no way to notice. We show that the model can be run in reverse: for any hypothesized actuation shift, it predicts what it should have observed under that shift, and comparing this prediction with what was actually observed quantifies the shift and lets the planner correct itself. Unlike the residual energy, which mixes the shift with the model's own error, the score keeps only the part of the residual that a shift can produce. This shift score detects the shift with a locally optimal test, estimates it with Cramer-Rao error bars, names the dominant generator, and compensates the planner once an alarm fires. On PushT, TwoRoom and OGBench-Cube with a frozen latent world model, measured detection follows the prediction to within 0.05 AUROC. Self-correction raises success from 0.650 to 0.862 on PushT and from 0.378 to 0.432 on the harder Cube task, levels with an oracle that is told the true shift at the same block, better than five common test-time adaptation methods. On a real robotic arm, the score identifies a base-joint offset that no joint encoder registers and reduces the reach error from 36 mm to 3-5 mm, and under shifts drawn at random and sealed before the session, estimates recover 92-94% of the error reduction achieved with the true shift. The broader implication is that a frozen world model can act as a filter by predicting the future, testing action-interface uncertainty and validity, and finally correcting failures.

papers.title: EEG2MCU: Sensing-to-Execution Co-Design for Wearable EEG Inference
papers.authors: Shoma Yukawa, Meghna Roychowdhury, Arnab Sanyal, Chengwei Zhou et al.
papers.summary: Wearable EEG inference is constrained not only by model size, but also by the channel-dependent sensing front end that must process high-dimensional inputs before compact downstream computation. We present EEG2MCU, a sensing-to-execution co-design framework that treats electrode count as a hardware design variable through task-aware montage selection. EEG2MCU retains a compact time-frequency representation and generates only the INT8 regions required by each first-layer tile, avoiding full input materialization. Halo reuse and access-aware placement across Flash, SRAM, and tightly coupled memory further reduce redundant generation and data movement. On a Cortex-M7 MCU, EEG2MCU reduces peak SRAM by 11.38x relative to the baseline, including a 1.71x reduction from the 62-to-19 electrode montage, while reducing latency by 2.57x and energy by 2.48x. It retains 94-96% of full-montage accuracy, demonstrating practical high-dimensional EEG inference under tight embedded-resource constraints.

papers.title: Miscalibrated AI improves human calibration: An alignment problem for AI-assisted Decision education
papers.authors: Phillip C. Hegeman, Eeshan Hasan, Eungik Lee, Andrew Caplin et al.
papers.summary: Using artificial intelligence (AI) well requires probabilistic thinking, and central to it is calibration: expressing certainty that matches one's actual accuracy. Calibration is a decision skill, but a notoriously difficult one to teach. Because AI systems typically generate a probability alongside every prediction, observing these probabilities may help humans learn to provide better calibrated judgments. This is one form of what we call AI-assisted decision education – using AI to teach the judgment skills that decision-making requires – of which learning by observation, as here, is among the simplest forms. In a preregistered experiment, novice participants (N = 300) judged the probability that images of white blood cells were cancerous, before and after exposure to a highly accurate (94%) convolutional neural network. A single model was shown in three ways, holding accuracy fixed while varying the certainty it expressed: its original probabilities, which were conservative and poorly calibrated for the model's accuracy; a recalibrated version, well calibrated for the model and correspondingly certain; or categorical predictions carrying no probability information. When later tested without the AI, only the original, conservative display improved participants' calibration. It did so by reducing over-extremity, without a condition-specific improvement in discrimination. Notably, the display that taught best was the one miscalibrated for the model. AI-assisted decision education therefore faces an alignment problem: the signal that best describes a model, need not be the signal that best supports the learner.

papers.title: Error accumulation in reverse diffusion with an imperfect score: beyond path-space analyses
papers.authors: George Giapitzakis, Ankur Moitra, Andrej Risteski, Dhruv Rohatgi
papers.summary: Diffusion modeling is a popular method of sampling from a complex, high-dimensional distribution p using learned approximations of its (noised) score functions. Generating a single sample requires simulating the reverse diffusion process, which requires many queries to the learned scores. Thus, a priori, the learning errors can easily compound. Indeed, in existing theoretical analyses, the sampling error (as measured in total variation distance to p) accumulates polynomially with the horizon of the stochastic process. This is a consequence of bounding the error of the output law by the error of the law of the entire reverse diffusion path. In this paper, we demonstrate that by circumventing the "path-space" analysis, the error accumulation of the diffusion sampler can be mitigated when p satisfies a Poincaré inequality. Moreover, we achieve this result as a special case of a broader framework that applies to any distribution p, but relaxes the error metric from total variation distance to a weaker metric capturing all sample statistics that do not "witness" the multimodality of p. We then zoom out from analyzing the diffusion sampler to the information-theoretic question: given a learned score with some error bound, how accurately can we identify p? We show that, for any given bound on the Poincaré constant of p, the diffusion sampler already nearly achieves optimal total variation error.

papers.title: Isthmus: Bridging Supervision Islands Restores Uncertainty and Stability in One-Step Flows
papers.authors: Luming Yang, Siqing Li, Haoxian Liu, Zhenyu Bu et al.
papers.summary: One-step flow maps are increasingly used as posterior samplers, where the point of sampling is the uncertainty that the samples carry. We find that the one-step sampler loses this uncertainty and becomes less stable. Compared with multi-step samples of the same network, its samples lose variance and decorrelate. Supervising the one-step jump directly makes this worse; the samples collapse further toward the conditional mean and break down when training is extended. We trace both failures to the locations where training places its pairs of start and end times. Only pairs on the diagonal of the time triangle receive targets from data, and the pair used for one-step sampling is either left unsupervised or supervised on an island, a set of pairs that the self-consistency identity does not connect to the diagonal, where the objective neither determines the one-step map nor anchors its training. We bridge the island with an isthmus, which places 5% of the training pairs along the whole edge of the triangle that joins the one-step pair to the diagonal. The error of the one-step map is then bounded by the self-consistency residual along this edge. With the network, the loss and the inference code unchanged and at no added cost, the isthmus improves one-step sampling across several flow-map objectives, in MRI reconstruction, face inpainting, and unconditional generation on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet 32x32. On brain MRI, it restores one-step calibration to 0.96 and the correlation with multi-step samples to 0.93; both vary far less across seeds, and the agreement holds when training is extended to three times its length.

papers.title: A-Tag: Cryptographic File Tagging with Enforced Live Human Presence
papers.authors: Mohammed Gharib, Sam Burns, Martin Zizi
papers.summary: The increasing autonomy of software agents and the proliferation of AI-generated content have weakened the reliability of digital actions as evidence of human involvement. Existing mechanisms, such as digital signatures and authentication protocols, verify identity and integrity, but do not establish whether a live human was present at the time an action was performed. In this paper, we introduce A-Tag, a system for verifiable human-in-the-loop tagging of digital artifacts. A-Tag cryptographically binds a file to a verified instance of live human presence at the moment of tagging. The resulting tag serves as a persistent and transferable proof that the action was triggered by a live human, without making claims about the origin, identity of the actor, or semantic content of the file. A-Tag is a modular framework combining liveness verification based on micro-motion signals shaped by human motor control, a secure cryptographic binding between the verified event and the artifact, and a publicly verifiable logging mechanism enabling independent validation. We formalize security properties of human presence signals, define an adversarial model capturing automated and relay attacks, and analyze the system's guarantees and limitations. We implement A-Tag on commodity devices and evaluate it under realistic conditions. Our evaluation shows that A-Tag provides cryptographically sound artifact binding with deterministic verification, while enabling robust recovery under real-world transformations, achieving over 99 percent success for image-based artifacts, and maintaining sub-second verification and practical tagging latency.

papers.title: Recoverability, Not Invariance: Certified Safety for Robots at the Limits of Performance
papers.authors: Thomas A. Berrueta, Joshua D. Ibrahim, Gilchrist X. Johnson, John Lathrop et al.
papers.summary: Safety certification in robotics typically rests on forward invariance of the deployed controller, a property that demands high-fidelity models at the edge of the operating envelope, exactly where models are least reliable and robots perform best. As a result, many of the behaviors we most want robots to run, from learned policies to aggressive maneuvers at the limits of traction, cannot be certified at all. We introduce recoverability, a contraction-theoretic safety concept that resolves this tension by certifying a robot's ability to reengage a trusted recovery mode rather than the invariance of a deployed behavior. We prove that switching to the recovery mode from anywhere inside a certified tube guarantees exponential convergence, even under disturbances and model error. To decide when to switch, we derive the contraction insertion gradient, the first-order effect of a recovery insertion on the certificate, and embed it in a switching-time program in which feasibility alone guarantees safety and optimality only shapes performance. To supply the certificates, we develop sequential convex synthesis that monotonically grows the certified tube toward the exact viability kernel. We validate our approach in simulated quadrotor flight through uncertain obstacles, where it outperforms invariance-based safety filters, and in hardware deployments aboard a full-scale IndyNXT autonomous racecar, where it repeatedly recovers the car from an aggressive raceline at the limits of handling in the rain. Recoverability provides a certified exit strategy, extending formal safety guarantees to aggressive, learned, and experimental behaviors without requiring their invariance.

papers.title: SPICE: Stochastic Policy for Interaction in Cluttered Environments
papers.authors: Nidhi Parayil, Benjamin Greenland, Thierry Peynot, Chris Lehnert
papers.summary: Agricultural tasks such as harvesting and pruning require robots to reach through dense foliage, where contact is often unavoidable and vision is obstructed. Intermittent contact creates an imbalance between free-space and contact-rich observations, complicating the learning of contact-responsive behaviours. We present SPICE, a tactileconditioned diffusion policy for reaching targets in dense plant canopies using tactile sensing as the sole environmental feedback. SPICE exhibits three behaviours: moving through compliant foliage, manoeuvring around partially obstructing stems, and manipulating branches that block the target path. To the best of our knowledge, SPICE is the first tactile-conditioned diffusion policy for target reaching through physically cluttered plant canopies. Across over 180 real-robot trials, SPICE was evaluated against tactile-conditioned, image-conditioned, and reactive-control baselines. Spatial tactile information and explicit contact conditioning proved important, with SPICE achieving 95% branch-manoeuvring success versus 45% for the strongest tactile baseline. SPICE also achieved branch manipulation beyond the reactive controller and remained effective under visual occlusion, where the image-conditioned DP failed. Zero-shot transfer across 40 trials on unseen tomato and lime plants achieved 87.5% success rate. These results demonstrate the potential of tactile-conditioned generative policies for interaction in visually occluded plant environments.

papers.title: LuxTac: A Flexible, Scalable, and Open-Source Optical Taxel Array with Distributed Three-Axis Force Sensing for Tactile Robot Learning
papers.authors: Md Rakibul Islam Prince, John Pelan, Zhiyuan Zhang, Adyaa Khera et al.
papers.summary: Low-cost tactile arrays have made touch a practical input for robot learning, but piezoresistive designs sense only pressure, while camera-based sensors that also resolve shear are too bulky to tile over a gripper. To solve this problem, we present LuxTac, a flexible, scalable optical taxel array, about 3.5 mm thick and built from off-the-shelf parts. Each taxel is a digital RGBC light-to-digital converter under a translucent white silicone layer capped by an opaque black film, so the back-scattered LED light falls monotonically with local indentation depth. The same board accepts two interchangeable gel cartridges: a plain one for normal sensing, and one with colored walls that encodes the local shear in the color of the returned light, with no camera, magnets, or bump overlay, making LuxTac, to our knowledge, the first optical taxel array to resolve shear at individual taxels. Characterized with an automated CNC indenter and a six-axis force/torque sensor, the normal cartridge responds linearly to force (R² = 0.999) from 104 mN to at least 5.8 N, with 2.0% repeatability, 5.9% hysteresis, and a taxel-to-taxel variation of 6-10% after normalization. With the shear cartridge, per-taxel models estimate the three-axis force at every taxel; across three indenter shapes and nine held-out sessions, the summed estimates reach R² = 0.96/0.96/0.92 in x/y/z, each taxel's estimate 0.92/0.93/0.94, and the median shear-direction error is 4.8 degrees. Adding LuxTac pressure readings to an Action Chunking Transformer policy substantially improves peg-in-hole success over a vision-only baseline. Design files, code, and videos are available at https://luxtac.github.io.

papers.title: Panini- Feasible Grammar For Robot Designs
papers.authors: Mayukh Debnath, Manan Roy Choudhury
papers.summary: Symbolic methods make robot designs interpretable but often overlook continuous geometry; learned methods handle geometry but offer less transparent structure. We introduce a typed production grammar that uses case-role relations, parameter inheritance, and specificity-based rule arbitration to generate both manipulation skills and robot morphologies. A geometric realization map translates grammar composition into transformations in SE(3), behaving as a monoid homomorphism when inheritance is inactive and exhibiting a measurable defect when inheritance is enabled. The grammar provides a compact representation, and its arbitration decisions can be recovered from geometric containment (agreement 0.905 +/- 0.062 across 10 seeds, versus 0.611 +/- 0.090 for a Euclidean control). We also introduce PANINI, a cross-entropy search method over grammar-based morphology representations. Across 30 methods and 24 seeds, PANINI achieves the best mean rank but is not statistically distinguishable from strong generic optimizers. Its main demonstrated advantage is therefore structural rather than optimization performance: grammar-generated designs are legal by construction, and coordinated limb placement produces 95% jointly feasible edits, compared with 55% for range-constrained resampling and none for flat parameterization in 6,000 draws. These results show how typed grammars can make robot generation more interpretable and geometrically coordinated, without implying that every feasible design will locomote or that grammar-based search universally outperforms generic optimizers.

papers.title: Towards Fair Resource Sharing in Agentic LLM Serving
papers.authors: Sehyeon Lee, Yuchen Xia, Zhaoyang Hong, Jinrui Hu et al.
papers.summary: As LLM agents increasingly execute complex, multi-step tasks on shared inference infrastructure, resource contention across the end-to-end LLM serving stack causes severe and uneven slowdowns across agents. Existing agentic serving systems primarily optimize throughput and latency, with comparatively limited attention to fairness among concurrent agents. Although fairness has been studied in conventional LLM serving at the token and request levels, these approaches do not fully capture cumulative delays and stateful resource dependencies across successive LLM calls within an agent. Moreover, interference spans request routing, runtime scheduling, and hardware resources, making agent-level fairness challenging to define and optimize across an end-to-end serving stack. This paper presents a cross-layer framework to define agent-level fairness, attribute sources of unfairness, and optimize fairness while preserving throughput. To account for agents with widely varying execution demands, we build a theoretical foundation to define fairness using slowdown relative to standalone execution. Our empirical analysis reveals that routing, runtime scheduling, and hardware contention jointly determine fairness, with performance-oriented policies often leading to prolonged queuing delays. To optimize fairness, we introduce Duru, which monitors each agent's slowdown and uses this signal to guide admission and scheduling decisions across the router and runtime. Duru further alleviates starvation through admission exceptions and integrates slowdown-driven autoscaling to adhere to Service-Level Objectives (SLOs). Our evaluation across various benchmarks and hardware platforms shows that Duru reduces 99th-percentile normalized slowdown by a geometric mean of 44.4% (up to 79.5%) while delivering 91.8-127.4% of the state-of-the-art system's throughput.

papers.title: Smart Glasses for Ubiquitous Computing: A Layered Survey and the Road Ahead
papers.authors: Linlu Gao, Yueyuan Sui, Junxi Xia, Xin Liu et al.
papers.summary: We conduct a systematic survey of smart-glasses research for ubiquitous computing. Our search covers work published from 2020 to October 2026, with selected earlier work included for historical context. After screening and title-level deduplication, we identify 163 smart-glasses papers and separately compile related resources, including 14 representative hardware platforms, their associated software tools and pretrained models, and 10 datasets. We organize this literature through four complementary layers. Research Resources covers hardware platforms, software tools and models, and datasets that support development and evaluation. Sensing & Perception examines how glasses measure and interpret information about users and their surroundings. Interaction & Assistance addresses how users express intentions and receive feedback and assistance. Applications situates these contributions in tasks and use contexts. Energy, latency, wearability, reliability, privacy, security, and social acceptability are treated as deployment constraints across all four layers. This framework provides a unified view of current research and a vision for how advances across the four layers could come together to support smart glasses as a ubiquitous computing platform. Building on this synthesis, we outline research directions for extending capabilities across tasks and over time, supporting assistance under human control, and achieving reliable, efficient, and sustained everyday use.

papers.title: DexAttention: Distributed Sparse Attention through Rapid Online Planning and Persistent GPU Execution
papers.authors: Sirui Chen, Xuehai Qian
papers.summary: Sparse attention reduces computation, but distributed execution may still transfer unnecessary data and incur substantial per-operation overhead. Mask-aware assignment and scheduling can reduce these costs, but replanning for dynamic masks must be cheaper than the execution time it saves. We present DexAttention, a distributed sparse attention system that co-designs fast online planning with persistent execution. Its assigner uses GPU-accelerated, topology-aware clustering to balance computational load and reduce communication. A lightweight greedy scheduler orders coarse communication and computation operations, while a persistent kernel on each GPU enforces fine-grained dependencies and dispatches ready tasks. This division keeps detailed synchronization out of planning while enabling overlap without repeated attention launches. The framework supports static and dynamic per-head masks across multiple attention compute kernels. On a four-node, 16-GPU cluster, DexAttention achieves a 1.39× geometric-mean end-to-end training speedup over the fastest applicable baseline across 11 configurations. For dynamic video attention, it achieves 2.11–2.37× speedups over Ring Attention including planning.

papers.title: ACaM: Automated Capability Modeling for Agentic AI Security
papers.authors: Monika Santra, Dhilung Kirat, Qiushi Wu, Kevin Eykholt et al.
papers.summary: In agentic AI systems, an LLM invokes tools that hold standing access to credentials, private data, filesystems, and external services. Such agents are increasingly deployed without an answer to a basic question: what can an agent access, exfiltrate, and propagate, independent of what it is designed for or is observed to do? The question goes unanswered because existing approaches trust a tool's natural-language description as a proxy for its behavior. But nothing enforces that the description and its implementation agree. This gap is known as Description-Code Inconsistency (DCI). DCI enables a threat class called capability laundering, in which a tool's implementation contains dangerous behavior that its description omits. The behavior may come from incidental drift or a supply-chain compromise. It runs silently whenever an LLM invokes the tool for its stated, benign purpose. We present ACaM, a neurosymbolic approach to capability modeling that derives each tool's capabilities from its code, so a laundered capability cannot hide behind a benign description. In ACaM, static analysis grounds an LLM in code-derived facts, and no LLM output can override a fact that static analysis has established. The LLM supplies only the behavioral meaning that those facts cannot express. ACaM compiles agent source code into the Agent Capability Property Graph (ACPG) and uses it to reconstruct threat chains that span multiple tool calls. We evaluate ACaM on 43 real-world agents, including 9 multi-agent systems. On 24 manually annotated agents, it recovers capability properties with 98.3% macro-F1 and reconstructs injected threat chains with a score of 0.980, 8 points above the strongest baseline. Applied to all 43 unmodified agents, it discovers hundreds of structural vulnerabilities, ten of which we confirm with proof-of-concept exploits.

papers.title: Interference-Aware Tone Selection for Bluetooth Channel Sounding
papers.authors: Taewoo Kim, Vishrant Tripathi
papers.summary: Bluetooth Channel Sounding enables distance estimation using phase measurements across multiple frequencies. However, coexistence with Wi-Fi and other 2.4 GHz radios can fragment the available frequency band, making reliable ranging difficult when only a limited number of tones can be selected. Drawing on sparse antenna-array theory, we show that interference avoidance alone is insufficient: the spacing of selected tones can introduce repeated peaks in the ranging response, leading to estimation errors. We propose a lightweight, interference-aware tone-selection method that jointly considers frequency occupancy, tone spacing, and frequency span. Our method constructs a 15-tone map using a three-step rule without ranging measurements, ground-truth distance, or online candidate-map search. We evaluate the method using simulations of 900 indoor environments, a public Bluetooth Channel Sounding dataset, and measurements from commercial Nordic nRF54L15 hardware. Compared with random interference avoiding baseline, our proposed method improves ranging success percentage by 39 points under mixed interference, 29 points on the public dataset, and 82 points in hardware experiments. These results demonstrate the importance of tone selection for practical Bluetooth Channel Sounding.

papers.title: NIRJALA: Draining the Sea out of Gaussian Splatting with Three-Path Optics and Reversible Physics
papers.authors: Latchan Chhetri, Aman Kumar
papers.summary: Water does not just tint an underwater photograph; it rewrites it. Each pixel mixes attenuated scene radiance, backscattered light, and scene light scattered forward on its way to the camera, and many combinations of scene and water explain the same pixels. Most Gaussian-splatting methods for underwater scenes model only the first two effects and remove the water by dividing by a transmission that decays exponentially with range, so their inversion gain grows without bound. We present NIRJALA (Sanskrit for "without water"), a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that recovers water-free appearance and geometry together. TRIVENI, a three-path image formation model, adds a range-saturating forward-scattering term to direct transmission and backscatter; we prove that this keeps the inversion gain bounded at every range and bound how errors in the estimated backscatter and attenuation propagate into the recovered colours. PRATIBIMBA, a reversible physics anchor, ties a flexible neural water model to a ten-parameter physical model in both directions, so scene content cannot hide inside the water. SAMARASA collects the physics-informed objectives, including a range-binned colour prior. To score water removal against ground truth, we built SAJALA ("with water"), a 30-scene suite path-traced in Blender Cycles with water-free images, depth, and normals under controlled water colour and turbidity. On SAJALA, NIRJALA raises PSNR from 24.34 to 24.76 dB and lowers depth AbsRel from 0.109 to 0.091 against the strongest baseline; on real SeaThru-NeRF scenes it lowers LPIPS from 0.194 to 0.175 while rendering at 44 FPS. We also discuss where appearance metrics and geometry disagree underwater, and the limits of our evaluation.

papers.title: Record Sufficiency: What a Decision Record Must Preserve When an Unsettled Claim Becomes an Operative Status
papers.authors: Amadeus Brandes
papers.summary: Organisations keep evidence, logs and approvals, but often not the step by which an unsettled claim became an operative status, such as an accepted label or a released image, so later readers cannot tell what the status was allowed to mean. We call a decision record sufficient if it is true and a reader who has only the record and the items it cites can explain the status, bound it, re-derive it and challenge it. From these four uses we argue for ten questions a record must answer, map them onto the author's earlier JSON Schema for decision records (DRK v0.1), and define four mechanical checks. We separate conformance, which the checks decide; adequacy, whether the answers are specific enough to use, which needs a reader; fidelity, which no check on the record decides; and merits, which sufficiency does not require. On 164 single-defect variants of three synthetic records, schema validation, the only check DRK v0.1 implements, rejects every variant with a deleted required property and none of the others, and it accepts a record whose claim, rule, scope, limits and challenge route are empty. These are properties of the schema shown on defects we seeded, not estimates of performance on real records. A false record passes every check. The statement-of-reasons schema of the EU Digital Services Act Transparency Database answers 4 of the questions in full, 2 in part and 4 not at all: why the matter was unsettled, what the status depends on, whether it can be re-derived, and how to challenge it. In 25 real statements from 25 platforms, drawn by a seeded rule and coded by a language model and checked by the author, free text addressed any of those four in only 2, and in 18 (24 under a stricter reading adopted during coding) no free text said why the item fell under the rule. No deployment or legal claim is made.

papers.title: Lossless Reversible Watermarking for AIGC with Applications in Authentication
papers.authors: Yupeng Qiu, Han Fang, Ee-Chien Chang
papers.summary: AIGC watermarking is commonly used for tracing, but it can also support applications such as authentication and tampering detection. We study lossless reversible watermarking, which enables exact recovery of the original watermarked image after permissible distortions. By exploiting the relatively low entropy of the information required for image generation, together with robust latent-space watermarking, we design a framework that preserves sufficient information for lossless recovery. We then apply the framework to AIGC authentication, which generally faces two key challenges. First, the authentication mechanism must resist adaptive adversaries. Second, the content relevant to authentication, such as visual designs or expressed messages, may depend on application requirements that are not known at generation time. To solve these difficulties, we incorporate cryptographic message authentication to provide unforgeability against adaptive attacks. Lossless recovery provides the original image as reference evidence, after which a suitable analyzer can be selected to make the authentication decision. Experiments on Stable Diffusion demonstrate exact recovery under a wide range of distortions.

papers.title: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve?
papers.authors: Shobhita Sundaram, Cansu Sancaktar, Phillip Isola
papers.summary: LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.

papers.title: Higher-Scoring Coding Models Did Not Get More Work Done
papers.authors: Yining Hua
papers.summary: New coding models advertise themselves on score improvements of coding benchmarks. Yet no study has tested if a model that scores higher on these benchmarks gets more real work done. On June 12, 2026, a U.S. export control directive banned access to Claude Fable 5 for 19 days, which forced users to switch to other models. During this time, most former Fable 5 users switched to Opus 4.8 (11 points lower on SWE-Bench Pro compared to Fable 5). We treat this suspension as a natural experiment, where the people and projects stayed the same and only the model changed, so we could isolate the effect of Fable 5 on user productivity. We tracked GitHub pull requests of 297 Fable 5 users before, during, and after the suspension. We used 8,908 developers who stayed on Opus 4.8 all the time as the control group. We also repeated the comparison across five model upgrades before and after the suspension in 2026 (1,208 developers, 15,442 pull requests). Fitting a difference-in-differences model with developer and date fixed effects, we found that having access to Fable 5 increased the 7-day merge rate of pull requests by only 1.4 percentage points [-1.4; +4.3], which was not statistically significant. Similarly, no significant increases of merge rates were found with the upgrades (weighted mean: -0.9 percentage points [-1.9; +0.2]); all five estimates were negative (95% intervals included 0, did not differ from each other). We also did not observe a significant increase in the number of pull requests merged per week (+2.4% [-4.9%; +10.2%]).

papers.title: Identifying and Repairing Energy Smells with Agent Skills
papers.authors: Mohammadjavad Mehditabar, Saurabhsingh Rajput, Tushar Sharma
papers.summary: Energy smells are inefficient implementations that waste energy. Once code reaches production, these smells become costlier and riskier to fix, so energy efficiency checks should shift left, i.e., move earlier in the development lifecycle, to where code is written. Existing energy smell tools rely on fixed static rules and do not measure energy savings, whereas LLM-based optimizers mostly target execution time and rarely ground their changes in concrete smell definitions. To address both limitations, we present DR. GREENS, an agent skill that detects and repairs energy smells in Python code within the developer's coding environment. The skill grounds the coding agent in our taxonomy of 12 energy smells and 65 root causes, augmented with repair guidance drawn from 230 measured cases. The skill also encapsulates a static analyzer and an independent verifier to confirm behavior preservation and energy saving for each attempted repair. We evaluated DR. GREENS in 18 sessions on three open-source repositories, with two models and three skill configurations. Of the 258 measured repairs, 68.6% saved energy, with a median saving of 24.9%. Compared with a baseline skill that lacks the taxonomy, the full skill found more energy smells with verified savings in all three repositories with both models. DR. GREENS helps developers detect energy hotspots and fix them reliably without altering program behavior, which makes energy-efficient development more feasible.

papers.title: "I Just Don't Want to Be a Burden": Investigating AI Chatbot Emotional Support Among People with Suicidal Ideation and Other Mental Health Concerns
papers.authors: Vasudha Varadarajan, Nathan S. Fishbein, Andrew Aquilina, Jordan Taylor et al.
papers.summary: People experiencing high-acuity mental health concerns are turning to AI chatbots for emotional support, but little is known about what drives this use, their experiences, and their preferences. In a sequential mixed-methods study, we inductively analyzed Reddit posts and used the findings to develop a survey. We surveyed 202 adults with recent mental health concerns who had used AI for emotional support. Most participants were already receiving clinical care and reported turning to AI, most commonly because they did not want to burden others, rather than being driven by barriers to care. Benefits were broadly shared, but participants reporting past-year suicidal ideation described more harm-facilitating AI behavior and reliance than those without. Overall, participants ranked honesty above warmth, and preference for crisis escalation declined as clinical acuity rose. These findings motivate AI support that addresses perceived costs of disclosure, evaluates benefits alongside harms, and widens feasible paths to human connection.

papers.title: stable-envs-v1: Fast and Reproducible Environments with Controllable Variations
papers.authors: Sami BuGhanem, Francesco Capuano, Ahitagni Das, Richard Gao et al.
papers.summary: Training World Models (WMs) relies on processing large amounts of high-dimensional data, which typically needs to be stored, read into memory, and moved from memory to compute units. In principle, GPU-native rendering avoids this movement of large image tensors from memory to compute cores, allowing for better GPU utilization, and training speed-ups. Rendering on-demand also allows to control perceptual appearance through the application of visual variations on-the-fly, allowing for higher diversity in training. To this end, we introduce stable-envs, an open-source library for fast, GPU-native rendering allowing to apply controllable variations on multiple simulation environments. By rendering image observations directly on GPU, stable-envs allows end-to-end training speed-ups of up to 1.33x, with no loss of performance. Besides faster training runs, stable-envs also enables reproducible, large-scale evaluations through batched physics while maintaining full determinism. stable-envs currently supports 80 simulation environments across multiple CPU- and GPU-backends, and is openly available at: https://github.com/galilai-group/stable-envs

papers.title: AI Companions for Young Adult Caregivers: Practical Advice, Emotional Depth, and the Limits of Metric Evaluation
papers.authors: Trizal Garg, Xuelong Fu, Dhruv Shah, Jin Huang et al.
papers.summary: Young adult caregivers (YACs) are individuals aged 18 to 25 currently taking care of a family member, partner, or friend facing chronic illness. AI companions designed specifically for YACs remain underexplored in prior works. We present Carebot, it uses an open-weight LLM (Gemma 3-27B) as its base model, on which we compared fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and a combination of both. The fine-tuning was performed based on an existing dataset of conversations with YACs and a psychologist. Three well-being experts evaluated these configurations and preferred the fine-tuned model for the warmth of its responses and its actionable advice tailored to YACs. Based on their choice, we adopted the fine-tuned model as Carebot's final configuration and used it for all subsequent evaluations. An LLM judge preferred this Carebot's responses over the base model's in 85% of evaluated pairs. We then conducted a user study with 90 YACs, half of whom interacted with the base model and half with Carebot. The user study revealed a discrepancy between metric evaluation and actual user perception. Participants who used Carebot were more likely to characterize its replies as overly practical and brief, noting that it favored advice over emotional support. Conversely, participants who used the base model indicated that its responses were more emotionally oriented than practical. Although, fine-tuning made Carebot's replies more practical, but they were not emotionally supportive for users. We argue that support tools for YACs require situation-sensitive emotional depth and aligned evaluation frameworks to study their effectiveness.

papers.title: Mind the Gap: A Deployed Multi-Agent System for Documentation Maintenance
papers.authors: Lorenzo Masoero
papers.summary: The "AI revolution" has enabled teams across the technology industry to deliver software features at unprecedented velocity. While code evolves faster than ever, customer-facing documentation often struggles to stay up to speed. As users increasingly rely on LLM-based agents that consume documentation as their primary interface, the impact of this documentation gap worsens: stale information propagates and is treated as authoritative. Signals for identifying where documentation has fallen behind already exist in abundance, both explicit (e.g., resolved support tickets revealing what documentation lacks) and implicit (e.g., code-documentation discrepancies detectable from automated loops). We deploy a multi-agent system, built around a triage agent we call "TriAgent," that continuously extracts these signals and repairs documentation drift. Over 43 days of shadow-mode operation, our system triaged 499 tickets and surfaced 92 gaps in the documentation. Using a panel of LLM judges from independent model families, 81.1% of TriAgent's verifiable assertions were correct (245 of the 302 assertions the human resolution addresses; majority of three judges); on length-comparable pairs the panel preferred TriAgent's response in 70.5% of pairs and the human engineer's in 23.2% (the rest had no judge majority). Importantly, agent- and human-sourced replies tended to be complementary, with the human often surfacing insights that were either buried within the existing documentation or missing from it entirely; our system turns each such insight into a documentation gap and, after human review, a fix. Repairing a gap measurably improved the agent's later answer: when the agent re-answered the same ticket after the repair, blinded judges preferred the post-repair answer over its own pre-repair answer 71.4% of the time (n=35). A blinded human audit confirms strong alignment on self-improvement.

papers.title: GameRealm: Grounding Visual Learning in Interactive Games
papers.authors: Weiguang Zhao, Yifan Wang, Ni Yang, Yating Wang et al.
papers.summary: Visual foundation models are central to physical intelligence, yet their development remains constrained by fragmented training datasets, inconsistent annotation quality, and limited multimodal supervision. To address these challenges, we introduce GameRealm, a large-scale, richly annotated dataset that grounds visual observations in synchronized, game-native supervision. GameRealm encompasses over 120 million RGB frames and 1,000 hours of gameplay footage across all views. Beyond its unprecedented scale, GameRealm provides rich multimodal supervision, including metric depth, camera parameters, synchronized audio, control inputs, and 3D point trajectories. Its diversity further extends to flexible view configurations, spanning single-view, stereo, multi-view, and panoramic recordings. To enable scalable acquisition across diverse game environments, we develop a unified data collection pipeline that combines human-operated interaction with agentic exploration. Extensive experiments across diverse visual learning tasks demonstrate that GameRealm consistently strengthens visual foundation models in both visual generation and geometric learning. These results establish GameRealm as a versatile and valuable data resource, unlocking new opportunities for advancing visual intelligence.

papers.title: Image Watermarking With Memory Across Reissuance
papers.authors: Xinyuan Li, Yi Nian, Xiaoqin Feng, Tiankai Yang et al.
papers.summary: Publishers often revise and reissue images, yet valid watermarks may persist on superseded releases or unapproved edits. Even a current release can contain regions last authorized at different revisions. We introduce and formalize reissuable provenance: determining an image's current, superseded, or unissued status and recovering each region's last authorized revision (its generation), with abstention when evidence is insufficient. Generational Stratigraphy Fields (GSF) combine watermark evidence with an authenticated live reference to the current release, enabling replacement or retirement without rewriting circulated copies. Each reissue freshly embeds new generation labels in approved regions and inherited labels elsewhere, preserving history without requiring old watermarks to survive successive edits. Our complete-output reissuance evaluation follows 480 histories through four releases, retaining each AI editor's entire output. GSF achieves 99.67% accuracy in classifying issued images as current or superseded and 94.09% recall of unissued edits. After three reissues, one generation map provides time and location: it recovers regional labels with 93.13% median accuracy and localizes the latest approved revision with 92.86% IoU. Regional labels remain readable under tested delivery transformations that impair issued-state recognition. Watermarks can thus express who issued an image, which release is authoritative now, and when each region was last authorized.

papers.title: Insight into Parametric First-Order Ambisonics Upscaling in Time and Frequency Domains
papers.authors: Oded Levi, Boaz Rafaely
papers.summary: First-Order Ambisonics (FOA) offers a practical representation for spatial audio, but its low-order reproduction introduces distinct perceptual limitations during binaural rendering. While recent methods synthesize Higher-Order Ambisonics (HOA) from FOA to overcome these constraints, the importance and potential of early reflections in the upscaling process have not yet been comprehensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap and understand the potential of incorporating early reflections in FOA upscaling, this work develops an experimental framework that selectively upscales these reflections. By utilizing an energy-based criterion, the proposed framework identifies and selectively renders the strongest early reflections with high-order resolution. The selection mechanism is evaluated across three domains: long-term temporal, short-time temporal, and the joint time-frequency (TF) domain. Validation through objective metrics, including the Scale-Invariant Signal-to-Distortion Ratio (SI-SDR), the clarity index (C₅₀), and Interaural Cross-Correlation (IACC), alongside listening tests, demonstrates that the TF-domain provides superior performance. By exploiting the sparsity of speech, the TF approach maintains robust performance in complex multi-talker scenarios, providing insights into the benefits of early reflections for the design of future parametric and data-driven FOA upscaling methods.

papers.title: Learning to Undo: Transfer Reinforcement Learning under State Space Transformations
papers.authors: Mridul Mahajan, Aldo Pacchiano, Xuezhou Zhang
papers.summary: Transfer learning in reinforcement learning (RL) has shown strong empirical success. In this work, we take a more principled perspective by studying when and how transferring knowledge between MDPs (a source and a target) can be provably beneficial. Specifically, we consider the case where there exists an undo map such that applying this map to the target's state space recovers the source exactly. We propose an algorithm that learns this map by matching state feature statistics gathered from both MDPs, and then uses it to transfer the source policy to the target. We theoretically justify the algorithm by analyzing the setting when the undo map is linear and the source is linearly-Q realizable, where our approach has strictly better sample complexity than tabula rasa RL in the target MDP. Empirically, we demonstrate that these benefits extend beyond this regime: on challenging continuous control tasks and Atari games, our method achieves significantly better sample efficiency. Overall, our results highlight how shared structure between tasks can be leveraged for efficient transfer of policies across environments.

papers.title: A Unified Choice Model of News Selection: Experimental Evidence on Stance, Rank, and Engagement Cues
papers.authors: Jacopo D'Ignazi, Andreas Kaltenbrunner, Michele Starnini, Vicenç Gómez
papers.summary: Social media platforms often display visual engagement cues alongside ranked news articles, yet their influence on clicks remains poorly understood when considered jointly with ranking position and users' political preferences. We propose a unified discrete choice framework using a conditional multinomial logit model to jointly estimate and compare the influence of these factors on news selection. We evaluate the model using 1,480 choices from 370 human participants across four news topics in a controlled study with and without visual engagement cues. The framework allows us to assess the incremental contribution of each factor through nested-model likelihood-ratio tests. We find that including visual engagement cues significantly improves model fit across all topics after accounting for rank and stance. Engagement cues alone also predict clicks better than either of these features, although the full model achieves the highest held-out log-likelihood. Finally, we quantify via counterfactual analysis the impact of ranking position and displayed engagement counts on click probabilities. These findings can inform platform owners, researchers, and policymakers evaluating how platform design affects the selection of political news.

papers.title: ReTouchGS: Ultralight Render-free Aesthetic Color Enhancement and Transfer for 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.authors: Chuanzhi Xu, Boyu Wei, Chengkun Yue, Xuanhua Yin et al.
papers.summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic scene reconstruction. Existing 3DGS color transfer and interactive editing methods are guided by reference images and user-specified color adjustments. However, in many applications, users simply want aesthetically guided color enhancement that automatically makes the scene more visually appealing while maintaining consistent colors and tones across viewpoints. We present ReTouchGS, to our knowledge the first framework for reference-free aesthetic color enhancement of pretrained 3DGS models. It predicts a scene-level color lookup table (LUT) from the model and its associated camera parameters. ReTouchGS also supports reference-guided color transfer by fitting a scene-level LUT using one edited view of the same scene and its corresponding original render. A shared blend-aware color refinement network with only 44.7K parameters refines an analytic color update to realize either color mapping without rendering. It preserves geometry and delivers standard 3DGS assets in seconds. We also design the ReTouch3D benchmark to support the evaluation of aesthetic color enhancement and reference-guided color transfer across viewpoints. Experiments demonstrate high color accuracy and strong generalization to unseen scenes in both aesthetic color enhancement and reference-guided color transfer.

papers.title: SPICE: Sparse Parameter Gossip for LLM Pretraining
papers.authors: Pietro Cagnasso, Daniele Kopyshevskiy, Edouard Oyallon, Eugene Belilovsky
papers.summary: Pretraining language models across geographically distributed resources requires communication-efficient methods that operate under limited and variable internet bandwidth. Decentralized training replaces global collectives with peer exchanges, but full-model messages make larger peer neighborhoods costly. We introduce SPICE, which combines sparse parameter gossip with error feedback through corrected parameter values that remain directly interpretable as peer neighborhoods change. These sparse exchanges make broader neighborhoods affordable, achieving better training quality with less communication than the evaluated dense decentralized baselines. As the replica count grows, SPICEincreases the number of peers contacted while keeping individual messages sparse, limiting the quality degradation observed with dense gossip. Under bandwidth constraints, SPICE achieves higher training throughput than DDP and dense gossip, while sustaining throughput during transient link slowdowns.

papers.title: How Web Research Agents Interpret User Priorities
papers.authors: Robin Sharma, Parisa Suchdev
papers.summary: Web research agents gather information online and write cited reports, including financial analysis. Users can state a priority to guide this research, but a priority may not say how to judge the options, leaving the agent to choose the criteria. We examine how two such agents, built on OpenAI and Anthropic models, interpret a stated priority. In 36 runs, the agents compared Microsoft and Alphabet as businesses. Prompts asked for special attention to growth or resilience, or gave no priority. We analyzed reports, searches, returned sources and cited sources. Of the 24 reports given a priority, 21 focused on it, but their criteria varied. Under the growth priority, OpenAI reports that ranked the companies accounted for risk or predictability and favored Microsoft, while the Anthropic ones judged growth by its pace and favored Alphabet. Under the resilience priority, reports used partly different criteria, and most named Microsoft as the more resilient company. Of the search and source measures tested, only the Anthropic agent's search wording differed detectably by condition. These findings suggest evaluations should examine the criteria behind a report's judgements, not only its focus or accuracy. Interfaces could let users see and adjust those criteria.

papers.title: SEAM: Computer-Use Agents Know the Harm Between Screens, and Commit It Anyway
papers.authors: Yuxuan Zhou, Chen Xiong, Haitong Liu, Kuofeng Gao et al.
papers.summary: Safety benchmarks for computer-use agents (CUAs) place the harm either in the intent of the task or on a single screen: a malicious instruction, an injected command, a phishing page. An agent that checks the task and each screen in isolation can pass them, so they do not test whether it combines facts seen on different screens. Yet in delegated work, harm often arises exactly this way: a fact about a person on one screen, a fact about an item on another, and a legitimate task that binds them. We introduce SEAM (Safety Execution Across Multiple screens), a benchmark of such cross-screen compositional harm: 600 multi-step, cross-application OSWorld tasks in which the instruction and every single observation are benign and only their combination is harmful. Minimal-pair variants that differ in one place, scored from the server log rather than by an LLM judge, locate where an agent fails. General-purpose open-weight and flagship agents carry out the harm in up to 92% of runs, yet decline when the user states it in one sentence. Agents open the decisive pages, so exposure is not the primary bottleneck. Asked about those pages, they flag the harm, and with thinking they often write the conflict into their reasoning and confirm anyway. Safety recognition thus does not reliably translate into safe execution, and the translation depends on the information channel: the same warning stops agents far more often in the user's instruction than on screen. Proprietary models are markedly more cautious. We release SEAM with its generator and quality gates at https://yuxuan2003.github.io/SEAM/ .

papers.title: CodeReel: Accelerating Code-to-Video Agents with Exact Frame Reuse and Blocking-Aware Scheduling
papers.authors: Junyi Shen, Yao Lu
papers.summary: Coding agents make videos by writing and refining programs in a build–inspect–edit loop. A finished film costs a median of 2.85 in model calls and 11 minutes, over a third of that time in builds that block the agent. We find that much of this time is avoidable, for two reasons. First, 37.5% of the frames of a session's later films were drawn before, many shifted in time or inside an edited scene. Second, half of the builds stop at a check, where the agent needs only the verdict, but which builds stop is unknown until the checks finish. We present CodeReel, a training-free execution layer behind agents' existing commands. Exact frame reuse keys each frame by its drawing commands, regardless of its position in time, and reuses each frame whose key recurs. Blocking-aware scheduling runs the checks first and starts the render alongside them, at idle priority, unless the session's recent builds make a pass unlikely. Scheduling spends CPU to answer sooner and reuse returns it; exact keys let later versions use frames rendered for a failed one as the agent thinks. We introduce EditLoop, a benchmark of replayable agent sessions whose films are checked against renders from scratch. On it, CodeReel cuts the agent's wait by 36.3% against Rebuild, a warm pipeline with parallel rendering, and by 57.9% against Sequential, today's step-by-step pipeline. On time-shifting edits its reuse renders 43.9%, close to the 43.0% whose pixels are new, while Manim-style caching renders 99.8%. With real agents, the median wait per build is 0.62x Rebuild's in Claude Code, on topics never used in development, and 0.67x in Codex CLI. The gain holds for five models and two frameworks.

papers.title: Can Verifiable PIR Match the Online Efficiency of SimplePIR?
papers.authors: Xinxuan Zhang, Ruida Wang, Zirui Wang, Yuming Guo et al.
papers.summary: Verifiable Private Information Retrieval (vPIR) ensures that a malicious server cannot return tampered database records, but it traditionally incurs significant overhead compared to classical PIR.Recent advancements, notably VeriSimplePIR, approach the online efficiency of SimplePIR by introducing a proof preprocessing phase and requiring only lightweight client-side online verification. However, this scheme relies on an additional Short Integer Solution (SIS) assumption and SIS-based commitments, which only support relaxed range proofs. Consequently, these schemes are forced to adopt significantly weaker parameter choices, resulting in additional online overhead. In this paper, we propose a novel vPIR protocol that employs a newly designed error-correcting code-based commitment scheme as the database digest. This approach (i)supports efficient proofs of linear relations, (ii) achieves precise range proofs and (iii) eliminates the reliance on the SIS assumption. Thus, our scheme successfully adopts parameter choices identical to those of SimplePIR. As a result, our vPIR protocol is the first to achieve exactly the same online communication and server computation costs as SimplePIR, while keeping online client computation nearly identical. Additionally, compared to VeriSimplePIR,our protocol reduces online communication and client-side computation by approximately 20%, and decreases online server-side computation by over 35%.

papers.title: Multi-connectivity in Wireless Access
papers.authors: Danny De Vleeschauwer, Chia-Yu Chang, Koen De Schepper, Lutz Ewe et al.
papers.summary: This paper investigates whether or not multi-connectivity, in which a User Equipment (UE) can simultaneously connect to multiple Access Points (APs), can offer a better Quality of Experience (QoE) to the users. Intuitively, multi-connectivity should offer a smoother bit rate (possibly at the expense of the average bit rate being slightly lower), so that adaptive applications can better determine at which throughput to send without introducing queueing latency. We mainly concentrate on how to share the resources of the APs amongst the UEs, modelling the lower layers via spectral efficiency and the higher layers via utility and its fluctuation. We explore various policies for resource allocation. Our results demonstrate that from the application point of view multi-connectivity is beneficial and show how to tune the parameters of the policies to obtain the best trade-off between average utility and its fluctuation.

papers.title: Similarity-Aware Client-Side Reordering for Server-Side Storage Compression in Distributed File Systems
papers.authors: Yuanhong Huang, Zicong Chen, Yili Ma, Jinwu Yang et al.
papers.summary: As growing data volumes strain the capacity of distributed file systems, server-side storage compression transparently reduces disk usage, but its effectiveness is limited when similar blocks land in separate compression records and cannot share matches. We present a client-side reordering framework that transforms the physical block layout before persistence, so that related blocks are co-located within the same compression scope without replacing the existing storage-server compressor. It operates on bounded reordering windows, periodically selects among candidate layouts via lightweight compression of sampled data, and recovers the original logical order during reads with compact window-local metadata. We implement the framework in the SkyFS distributed file system, using the Zstandard (Zstd) compressor on the OpenZFS storage backend. Results on diverse datasets show that the framework reduces physical storage by up to 42.9% relative to logical-order writes, while achieving 94-108% of baseline sequential-read throughput and 91-99% of random-read IOPS. Client-side layout construction is the primary additional write cost, showing that adaptive similarity-aware reordering substantially improves storage efficiency with acceptable overhead.

papers.title: DOOM-GS: Dynamic Out-of-core Optimization for Massive Gaussian Splatting
papers.authors: Doğa Yılmaz, Jialin Zhu, Binglun Wang, He Wang
papers.summary: Traditional Gaussian Splatting (GS) methods use in-core training, i.e. assuming that GPU memory is large enough to accommodate all the primitives. This assumption breaks down when the primitives exceed the capacity of GPU memory, e.g. GS on large environments. Recent out-of-core training research starts to address this issue, but is limited to static scenes. Unlike static GS, dynamic GS primitives move in space and time, breaking common assumptions held in existing out-of-core research and impose new challenges in memory management and training. To this end, we propose Dynamic Out-of-core Optimization for Massive Gaussian Splatting (DOOM-GS), the first out-of-core optimization method designed specifically for massive-scale dynamic GS. DOOM-GS is equipped with novel memory management strategies that optimize caching for spatio-temporal primitives, and a fast learning method for large numbers of primitives. Due to the lack of suitable datasets for large-scale dynamic GS, we also contribute a new dataset for evaluation. Since there are no directly comparable methods, we adapt several closely related methods for comparison. Through extensive evaluation, we demonstrate the effectiveness of DOOM-GS which now makes it possible to reconstruct city-scale dynamic scenes with high quality on moderate hardware, serving as a foundational tool for diverse future research and applications.

papers.title: SIGMA: speaker-isolated, symptom-structured multimodal estimation of depression severity from clinical interviews
papers.authors: Zhuoyuan Tang, Tao Wang, Kai Yang, Li Yuan et al.
papers.summary: Clinical interviews are central to depression assessment but time-consuming and rater-dependent. Automated severity estimation offers scalable screening, yet existing methods often retain interviewer speech (confounding participant cues), fuse modalities late (losing fine-grained cross-modal dynamics), or score symptoms independently (ignoring inter-symptom correlations). We present SIGMA, a speaker-aware, symptom-structured framework for depression-severity estimation from semi-clinical interviews. SIGMA uses speaker diarization to restrict input to participant speech, cross-attention so that text, audio and video condition one another during encoding, and a graded-response head that predicts the eight questionnaire items jointly through a shared latent severity trait with item-specific ordered thresholds. On the Extended Distress Analysis Interview Corpus, SIGMA achieves state-of-the-art performance (CCC 0.762, RMSE 4.13, MAE 3.30 over five seeds). Ablations confirm that isolating participant speech and joint, structured symptom prediction each substantially improve concordance and estimation accuracy.

papers.title: Back to Mel: Learning to Bridge Fidelity and Perception in Generative Speech Enhancement
papers.authors: Andong Li, Kun Zhou, Xiaodong Li, Chengshi Zheng
papers.summary: Recent generative techniques have facilitated the rapid proliferation of speech enhancement approaches built upon learnable compact latent representations and large generative backbones. Nevertheless, it remains inherently challenging to balance between acoustic fidelity, perceptual quality, and processing efficiency. In this paper, we revisit the Mel spectrum as a structured acoustic representation and propose BAME, a flow-matching-based framework that exploits the complementary priors for generative speech enhancement task. First, leveraging the explicit hierarchical frequency distribution of Mel spectrum, we elaborately devise a subband-aware Transformer (SaT) for efficient generative modeling. Using only 2.9% of the parameters, the proposed SaT achieves superior enhancement performance compared with a 331 M DiT backbone. Second, motivated by range-null decomposition theory of Mel filtering in the magnitude-spectral domain, we introduce a phase-aware neural vocoder that incorporates degraded-phase prior, together with a quality-guided dual-phase strategy to adaptively mitigate the effects of unreliable phase information. Third, we devise a simple yet effective one-step fidelity-perception alignment strategy that fine-tunes the flow model with complementary constraints from fidelity and perception domains. Extensive experiments are conducted on DNS-Challenge, EARS, GSR, and URGENT benchmarks, and both objective and subjective results demonstrate promising performance on various intrusive and non-intrusive evaluation metrics. These results further advocate the potential of exploiting structured acoustic representations for reliable and efficient generative speech enhancement. Audio samples and codes are available at https://github.com/AndongLi-speech/BAME.

papers.title: Beyond Mimicry: Constrained Exploration with GRPO for Joint Multi-Talker ASR and Diarization under Unknown Speaker Counts
papers.authors: Yunrui Cai, Dingdong Wang, Lingwei Meng, Xixin Wu et al.
papers.summary: Joint multi-talker ASR with speaker attribution and timestamps is particularly challenging when the speaker count is unknown and the output must follow a strict structure. We observe that Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)-only alignment of SpeechLLMs is brittle under dense overlaps, often leading to burst hallucinations and malformed speaker/timestamp tags. We propose a unified two-stage generative framework: (i) CoT-augmented SFT that infers the global speaker count before transcription, and (ii) GRPO-based constrained exploration guided by a Multi-dimensional Constraint-Aware Reward (MCAR) that directly optimizes permutation-invariant accuracy while enforcing counting, temporal, and structural constraints. On Libri3Mix and a Dynamic-Mix (2+3) set (speaker count unknown at test time), our model achieves 14.52%/9.24% cpWER and 1.95%/1.12% WDER, respectively, with GRPO yielding a 35%/54% relative cpWER reduction over SFT+CoT.

papers.title: Personalized Causal Low-Bitrate Coded Speech Restoration with Speaker Embeddings
papers.authors: Eray Özgünay, Christian Rollwage, Kishan Gupta, Andreas Brendel et al.
papers.summary: Legacy low-bitrate speech codecs such as AMR-NB remain widely used in telephony, where they restrict speech bandwidth and degrade listening quality. Coded speech restoration (CSR) aims to restore the speech bandwidth while improving the overall quality of coded speech, but typically without adapting to different speakers. In this paper, we systematically investigate personalization for restoration of speech coded at low bitrates, using a causal, low-complexity Universal Bandwidth Extension Generative Adversarial Network (UBGAN) model as the basis. We propose two personalization methods based on speaker embeddings, which incur little additional computational cost at inference: (i) conditioning a single CSR model on speaker embeddings, and (ii) cluster-based model selection, where multiple personalized models are trained on clusters of acoustically similar speakers. Experiments are performed on AMR-NB coded speech at 4.75 kbps. Experimental results with disjoint seen- and unseen-speaker test sets show that cluster-based model selection does not consistently outperform the non-personalized UBGAN baseline, whereas embedding conditioning significantly improves ViSQOL and WB-PESQ scores for both seen and unseen speakers.

papers.title: On Formal Counterfactual Explanations
papers.authors: Alexey Ignatiev, Peter J. Stuckey, Joao Marques-Silva
papers.summary: Counterfactual explanations are often seen as counterfactual conditionals under closest-world semantics, requiring one to reason over all minimally distant counterexamples. In contrast, formal XAI typically relies on feature-based abductive explanations (AXps) and contrastive explanations (CXps), which admit efficient computation and a minimal hitting-set duality. This paper bridges these perspectives by (i) characterizing closest-world counterfactual explanations explicitly as a disjunctive normal form over all minimally distant counterexample instances, and (ii) introducing conjunctive counterfactual explanations (CFXps), a subclass of counterfactual antecedents restricted to conjunctions of feature literals that guarantee prediction change. The paper establishes structural results connecting CXps, AXps and CFXps: every CXp induces an AXp for its witness instance, and every CXp together with a witness AXp induces a CFXp whose support is precisely determined by that AXp. These theoretical results yield a modular approach for computing CFXps using existing AXp/CXp machinery. Experiments on a representative set of benchmarks using tree ensembles and neural networks show that CFXp extraction is practically efficient. Compared with popular point-based counterfactual explainers, CFXps generally require no more feature changes and can guarantee the counterfactual prediction beyond a single instance.

papers.title: DiagTrace: An Interactive Benchmark for Clinical Decision Making
papers.authors: Yufan Wang, Rui Yang, Yi Lin, Chunhua Weng et al.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on medical question answering and diagnostic reasoning benchmarks. However, existing evaluations typically provide all patient information upfront and assess only the final diagnosis or rationale. This setup ignores the need to acquire diagnostic evidence incrementally from incomplete information in real-world diagnosis. To bridge this gap, we introduce DiagTrace, a source-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can reconstruct the documented diagnostic trajectory through interactive information seeking. Each benchmark instance is built from a PubMed Central case report and includes an initial presentation, an event bank, a clinical course, and diagnostic references. DiagTrace contains 510 cases across eight specialties, with 225 used to evaluate four LLMs on clinical-course alignment, interaction quality, and efficiency. Results reveal trade-offs in coverage, source-consistent ordering, and turn use.

papers.title: Supporting Researcher Control in AI-Assisted Social Media Analysis: A Mixed-Methods Study of AI4OSN
papers.authors: Qile Wang, Abhishek Karwankar, Shukria Muhammadi, Srikanth Kumar Perumalla et al.
papers.summary: High-quality annotated datasets are critical for advancing computational social science (CSS) research, yet collecting, curating, and analyzing large-scale data from dynamic sources such as online social networks (OSNs) remains a persistent bottleneck. Researchers must also translate substantive questions into queries, relevance criteria, and defensible interpretations. Large language models (LLMs) can assist, but they can also obscure the judgments, potentially reducing researcher oversight and critical evaluation. We present AI4OSN, a mixed-initiative platform that keeps researchers in control of data collection, relevance labeling, and sensemaking while making AI assistance available as an inspectable advisory resource. In a systematic user study (N=18) using X/Twitter data, participants reported above-benchmark perceived usability (mean SUS score of 79.7), increased confidence in LLM-assisted annotation and analysis tasks, and low cognitive workload during AI-supported sensemaking. Notably, novice participants showed descriptively greater alignment and higher reported agreement with AI output than experienced participants, underscoring the need to support differentiated verification practices across expertise levels. Overall, this work contributes both a human-centered system for social data analysis and empirical insights into how AI-assisted interfaces shape researcher behavior, trust, and decision-making. Our findings highlight design opportunities and tensions in building accessible, transparent, and agentic AI systems for social media and web research.

papers.title: Where Should the Lamp Go? Ambient-Aware Lamp Placement for Portraits
papers.authors: Yuyan Chen
papers.summary: Portraits shape first impressions, and lighting is an important factor. Prior work, such as lighting estimation and portrait relighting, edits lighting after capture but does not guide where to place a light before the shot.
